I am 65 this year, and I have never been to school, but I know every ridge and furrow of my 7 mu of land in Quzhou better than any words on paper. The wheat I sowed last October is waking up from winter sleep now, so this spring my main job is to nurse it to harvest. I will top-dress nitrogen at green-up and again at jointing, irrigate three times if the sky stays dry, and spray twice for aphids and rust. I grow an improved wheat variety that the village extension man recommended years ago—it stands well and gives a stable harvest. As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant hybrid maize on the same 7 mu. I do not deep-plough for the maize anymore; I seed straight into the wheat stubble with no-tillage. It saves me diesel and precious days, and the yield is just as good if I keep the weeds down. For fertilizer, I will spread about 18 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium per mu for the wheat, and roughly 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu for the maize. The maize will get two irrigations and one or two sprays for stem borers. I do not mess around with vegetables or cotton—the market is fickle and my back is not young. Wheat and maize are safe. The grain station buys them, and I can store what my family needs.
